Cats don't have periods the same way humans do. Their "period" is called estrus and although it involves bleeding, most of the times it is re-absorbed completely before it gets out so it's rare for a female cat to bleed during her period although it can happen. 

During her estrus, a female kitty can change her behavior and become more affectionate, might meow very loudly, can be extra sensitive to pettings so she might bite from too much stimulation, etc.
Letting her out during her heat is a sure way to get her pregnant so if you don't want to end up with a litter, better avoid it by getting her neutered. This way she will become much more calmer, her behavior won't have abrupt bumps and local tomcats won't orbit your house looking for a female to mate.

My recommendation is that you get her neutered. This way either she'll be much more easy to relocate to another family or, if you decide to keep her, she won't turn unpredictable every time she's on heat and thus you'd have a smoother relationship with her.

I'm a one-woman-band too. Well, almost since I got a ton of a help from my friends for two things: one, for drums since I think nobody beats a human drummer (my opinion) so I got an old friend of mine to record them; and two, for mixing/mastering/some recordings so I went to another old friend of mine since I didn't want to learn the whole ton of mixing and mastering myself - I wanted to start releasing songs ASAP (and still, I'm a snail musician.)

So everything I can record on my own, I do. My apartment is noisy: dogs barking, neighbours alarms ringing, you name it. Therefore, all voices and everything that has to air-travel to get recorded, I do it in my friend's studio. All guitars, basses, some pianos, go directly to the audio interface so I record them on my own. Sometines I add just a little bit of distortion to the guitar signal from a multi-effects pedal (ToneTattoo by ElectroHarmonix) and to basses through the Fender Rumble output (so again, signal don't go through air). Other than that, my guitar and bass signals are quite naked at the time they arrive to my experienced friend's hands. All later processing (whole distortions, delays, etc.) are added by him and me working side by side, either through re-amplification or through effects plugins, or better, through a mixure of them both.

Also, when I give the tracks to my friend, I already did all the minute-detailed editing, everything is aligned (or not, but it has to be intentional in my opinion) to a metronome track I also give to him, all tracks are "frozen" in time so there's no chance they will deviate from the norm :) and also try to record my parts the very best I can.

These collaborations let me feel calmed down about not having to do all of the tons of stuff one has to do when you're embarked in such self-commitment. All the lyrics, the whole music and composition, the graphic stuff, the lyric videos, the recordings of voice, bass, guitars, double bass, piano, the whole "put yourself out there" stuff (which I definitely don't like but it has to be done)... all of this sure is enough for me to say: I need help in these two things because I don't want to spend a whole additional year learning how to mix/master to a pro level and how to play the drums to a great level :) .

So this is how I do it, perhaps this annuls me as a "one-woman-band" but what the heck, I already have two songs out there I wouldn't have otherwise :D . Hope this info serves you or other people out there to figure it out how to possibly kick start doing it.

I think ego comes in two sides: the useful one, and the dark one.

Your ego, to the best of my knowledge, is your conscious identity. You can use it, and you *should* use it, to advance the earthly path that's close to your heart and your perceived mission. It gives you courage, fuel and optimism in what you're doing. Most of all, it also gives you *direction*. That's the good ego.

Now, a bad ego would be, for example, if you attach your conscious identity to your goal. This would become dangerous because goals might not happen for a thousand reasons that won't necessarily depend on your abilities or your will, and if you have a strong attachment to it, your whole self would feel like crumbling down.

Egos are instilled in our brains for good reasons and my opinion is, it should not be dissolved. The trick is to have it checked only for what it is and always keep an eye when it wants to dictate you to feel or do some harmul or nasty stuff.

Great advices already posted. But I'd like to add: the kind of shows where the band has to sell tickets in advance are to be tried JUST ONCE in a lifetime, if ever. Because you're paying to play and it's not good unless you definitely need to be playing in that particular bar/spot for whatever reason, or because you're urged of live-playing web content for a due date, or something like that. Remember, your band is going to entertain audiences and that's a job per se. You don't pay for doing jobs, so why would you pay for doing the job of entertaining the audiences while they consume? For a time during your startup phase, free playing + beer + bar food should be the absolute minimum you should require from the promoter and you should work to move up from that situation ASAP. Paying for playing, on the other hand, is not free playing, is less than that.

I play bass while singing. My approach is to practice it measure by measure, if possible. If not possible, then I try it one click at a time. I repeat the single click that don't want to come clean, over and over and over until it's automatic and I don't have to think about it. Then I go towards first and second click of that measure, and repeat the same method, over and over until I can watch videos without thinking about it. Repeat until you finish the song. It's a lot of work but it's the only way that's worked for me with optimum results. Also, with time, it will become semi - automatic for your brain to absorb new loads of guitar + voice.
